stories.title: AI Finds the Bug That Humans Missed for Fourteen Years
stories.story:
The bug had been hiding in plain sight since 2012. PHP — the open-source scripting language that quietly powers roughly 70% of the world's websites, from WordPress blogs to Wikipedia — carried two memory-safety flaws that no human auditor had ever caught. This week, an AI did.

Researchers at security firm Wiz and a separate firm called Calif, working independently but using the same tools — OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol and Google's Gemini 4 Argon — surfaced the vulnerabilities this summer. Both flaws allow an attacker to execute their own code remotely on any server running PHP, unauthenticated. One of them exposes the memory of running PHP worker processes. The other corrupts shared server state. Together they were rated 9.2 out of 10 on the CVSS severity scale; one private firm rated them a full 10. The PHP Foundation, caught understaffed and aware that publishing vulnerability details also hands attackers a roadmap, issued emergency patches on October 21 and urged every operator to update immediately. Amazon Web Services reported evidence of exploitation attempts on a honeypot as early as October 17 — before public disclosure.

What makes this more than a routine patch cycle is the mechanism of discovery. The PHP Foundation acknowledged that a developer had noticed the first hints of one flaw in 2024, but the fix stalled for two years amid technical complexity and thin resources. AI did not find a new bug so much as it finished a job humans couldn't. That distinction matters enormously. If AI systems can now reliably close the gap between 'someone suspects a flaw exists' and 'the flaw is confirmed and exploitable,' then the economics of both defense and offense in cybersecurity shift at once — defenders patch faster, but so do attackers move to exploit before patches propagate.
stories.hook: The scariest part isn't that the bug existed for fourteen years — it's that AI found it before the defenders finished their coffee.
stories.source: Wiz Research / CyberScoop / ABC News Australia

stories.title: The Merger That Would Swallow Corporate History
stories.story:
The logic of Elon Musk's empire has always been vertical integration carried to an absurd extreme — cars that generate energy, rockets that reuse themselves, satellites that beam internet to the cars. This week, that logic found its terminus. On Tuesday's earnings call, Musk confirmed that SpaceX and Tesla have each formed special committees of independent directors to explore a merger that analysts estimate could produce a combined entity worth between $3.5 and $5 trillion, which would rank as the largest corporate combination in history.

The strategic rationale is not trivial. SpaceX already owns xAI, the company behind the Grok chatbot. Tesla is deep into autonomous vehicles and humanoid robots. Both companies are jointly building a semiconductor fabrication plant — Musk's so-called Terafab — to supply chips to each. A merged entity would own the full stack: energy storage, propulsion, satellite connectivity, AI compute, and the robots that might one day run on all of it. As one Morningstar analyst noted, Tesla's battery and solar manufacturing could directly feed SpaceX's ambition to put data centers in orbit, where there is no power grid to strain.

The catch is structural. Because Musk leads both firms, he is legally a conflicted party and has recused himself from the committees. More importantly, any deal would require approval from 50 percent of all Tesla shares outstanding — not merely those cast — a deliberately high threshold. SpaceX shares jumped 10 percent on the news. Tesla's rose too, even as the company reported operating profit down 56 percent year-over-year. Markets are pricing in the dream, not the difficulty.
stories.hook: The deal isn't done, but the committees are meeting — and that's how history-sized mergers begin.

stories.title: Turkey's Central Bank Holds at 37%, Betting Discipline Over Geopolitics
stories.story:
Today the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey held its benchmark one-week repo rate at 37 percent — a decision that sounds routine until you trace how the country got here. Markets had penciled in a cut to 36 percent, expecting the slow grind of disinflation to finally give policymakers room to ease. Instead, the committee held firm for a sixth consecutive meeting.

The backstory is a remarkable reversal of fortune. For years, Turkey ran the opposite playbook: President Erdoğan pressured the central bank to keep rates artificially low even as inflation tore through 80 percent, operating on the eccentric theory that high interest rates cause rather than cure inflation. The lira collapsed, household purchasing power was gutted, and foreign capital fled. After Erdoğan's re-election in 2023, orthodox economics made a quiet return. The bank raised borrowing costs from 8.5 percent all the way to a peak above 42 percent, rebuilt some credibility, and began a cautious cutting cycle. By January 2026, the rate had come down to 37 percent — and then stopped.

What stopped it was energy. The Middle East conflict sent oil prices surging, threatening to reignite inflation just as Turkey was beginning to breathe easier. Turkey's CPI still sits above 31 percent, but the central bank is holding out a real yield of roughly 5.5 percentage points above inflation — a deliberate buffer designed to keep the lira attractive and foreign capital in place.

The implied next chapter is delicate. Markets forecast the rate falling to 35 percent by year-end and to the low twenties by 2028. But that path depends entirely on energy prices stabilizing and the Fed's own tightening cycle — now pricing in another hike on October 28 — not pulling capital back toward dollar assets. Turkey's decade of monetary chaos burned credibility that takes years to rebuild. Today's hold is the central bank saying it won't repeat the mistake.
stories.hook: The easiest thing a central bank can do is cut rates when everyone expects it to — the hard thing is not to.
stories.source: Turkish Minute / TCMB Press Release / Trading Economics
